dharana.rendering: Let one cast the gaze over a place free of trees, hills, walls and the like. As the mental state dissolves there, the fluctuations of the mind cease.
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer (as printed in Wallis's concordance); not a quotation.
dharana.commentary_note: Singh: when the mind rests on a vast vacant space without the support of any definite object, its thought-constructs stop, and the light within makes itself felt. Abhinavagupta quotes the first line in his Parātrīśikā commentary as an entry into Bhairava-consciousness. Singh calls the fixed gaze into open space dṛṣṭibandhana-bhāvanā and classes it as śāmbhavopāya.
dharana.instruction: Rest your gaze on a wide, empty view and let the mind go quiet with it.

seat.label: Any steady, comfortable position (school addition)
seat.summary: Any steady, comfortable position facing an open view: a field, a beach, a wide sky, or a large empty wall if nothing else is available.
seat.honesty: School addition. Verse 60 does not specify a body position. The seat is a convenience so the dharana can be practised; it is not part of the technique and makes no claim of tradition.

points: a wide, open expanse with no objects to catch the eye
geometry.summary: Not a body shape. The map is a wide, empty view: open land, water or sky with nothing for the eye to hold on to.
geometry.svg_hint: a single horizon line across an empty page
geometry.honesty: Geometry records the dharana's own map of attention, not a body shape. Locations marked 'commentarial' come from commentary, not from the verse.

reaction.name: Let the eye go wide
reaction.summary: School metaphor only: the eye finds nothing to grab, and the mind's churning loses its handholds. Not a biochemical or medical claim.

breath.lands_in: wherever the breath naturally ends; this door places nothing on the breath
breath.cue: Natural breath. Count about four in and four out only if it helps you settle, then let the count go. No forced hold.
breath.honesty: The counts are an optional school pacing aid, not part of the verse. Hold is always 0: this school never adds a deliberate breath-hold.

orientation.cue: Face the widest, emptiest view available
orientation.gravity: Let the floor or chair carry the body completely; there is no posture to hold
orientation.gaze: Eyes open, resting on the open expanse; blink freely
orientation.degrees_hint: No angle target: the VBT gives no posture for this dharana

attention.primary: A wide, empty expanse with nothing for the eye to hold

adiyogi.verse_paraphrase: Let one cast the gaze over a place free of trees, hills, walls and the like. As the mental state dissolves there, the fluctuations of the mind cease.
adiyogi.method_summary: Find a wide, open view (open land, water, sky) without trees, hills or buildings in the foreground. Let the gaze rest on the openness without picking any object. Let the mind go quiet with it. Blink normally.

honesty.disclosure: Door 037 follows Vijñāna Bhairava Tantra dharana 37 (verse 60) in Jaideva Singh's numbering. The door-to-dharana index is a School of 112 Doorways teaching device. Singh's sequence is one edition's count, not an ancient one-to-one canon. The seat, counts, reaction and beat scripts are school additions.
honesty.notes: pairing_type is school_device: the dharana is the content, while the door index, seat and pacing are the school's.
flags: Door index = Jaideva Singh dharana number: Door 037 is dharana 37, verse 60. Other editions number differently (see dharana.numbering_variants).

The English is a school paraphrase, not a quotation from any translator.

safety.pain_rule: Pain is information. Pause, regress, or exit. Never push through sharp pain.
safety.open_seat_alternate: This door needs no particular posture: sit on a chair, sit on the floor with support, or lie down. Eyes may stay open.
safety.contraindication_notes: General practice caution only; not medical advice. Never look at the sun. Blink freely; this is a soft, wide gaze, not a stare. If anything feels distressing (dizziness, agitation, strong emotion), stop, open the eyes and rest attention on the feet and the floor.
